rating.reasoning_summary: This strand explores internet usage as a coping mechanism and the struggle to balance online/offline existence. The boundary object is 'being extremely online' itself—oscillating between internet-as-refuge (from school trauma, loneliness) and internet-as-trap (disembodiment, compulsion, parasocial distance). The arc is dialectical but circular: participants recognize the pattern (online = escape from pain → online = new source of pain → need to touch grass → return online) but lack a clear resolution. While there's shared vocabulary ('disembodied mental space,' 'touch grass,' 'Cassandra device'), the discourse doesn't evolve toward actionable frameworks—it's more confessional repetition than knowledge production.

essential_tweets.annotation: Origin: Framing 'extremely online' as a coping mechanism (2019 baseline)
Core trauma narrative: Internet as escape from school-induced disconnection from body/self
The dialectic emerges: 'Touch grass' as ironic recognition of internet-induced disembodiment
Reversal point: Internet becoming 'cringe,' reality as new escape (2023)
Peak despair: 'Cassandra device' framing, comparing to happier offline friends
Compulsion cycle articulated: posting/scrolling as addiction loop
Somatic response: 'Disembodied mental space egregore' + literal grounding (bare feet, bonsai)
Acceptance of different online habits; recognizing personal limits with presence
Current state: Still online, still coping, but with more self-awareness ('tending to feelings instead of running to distractions')

title: From coping to “Cassandra device”: the online spiral
summary:
The most quotable gut-punch was @mykola calling the phone “a nightmare Cassandra device” and saying they feel like they live in “3024” compared to their happier offline friends—like everyone else got out and you’re still stuck staring at the warning lights. That vibe reframed the whole convo from “lol chronically online” to “wait, this is actually messing with our nervous systems.”

The thread’s arc is basically: internet-as-life-raft → internet-as-quicksand → awkward attempts at “touch grass” solutions. It starts with @goblinodds (2019) treating “being extremely online” as a coping mechanism, then @inkolore_ (May 2023) supplies the trauma backstory: school wrecks your relationship to your body and agency, so of course kids flee to screens—taking phones away won’t magically make them healthy. @octopusyarn (June 2023) turns “touch grass” into a somatic thesis: online life flattens and accelerates you into paranoid feedback loops, so grounding is literally the point. By late 2023 @inkolore_ flips it—“the internet is becoming cringe so I might escape from it with reality”—and in Jan 2024 @danielbrottman draws the key distinction: “wholesome onlineness” vs “coping/avoidant onlineness,” even when you genuinely love being extremely online like @tasshinfogleman.

After the @mykola peak-despair moment (Jan 18, 2024), the energy kind of diffuses into receipts of the compulsion cycle: @lumpfished names the posting/replying/scrolling loop as addiction, then later describes getting pulled into a “disembodied mental space egregore” and tries to break it with absurdly literal grounding (bonsai seeds, bare feet on freezing earth). The thread doesn’t “solve” anything, but it does land somewhere more usable: @oloal admits some people are genuinely invigorated by all-day posting, but for them it kills presence—so they experiment with limits; @connerdelights suggests lists/saved searches to escape the infinite feed; @XyraSinclair ends on a messy, honest compromise: tweeting feels like “accruing aliveness points,” but they’re also coding again and “tending to feelings” instead of sprinting to distractions. Why care: it’s a map of how “being online” quietly shifts from shelter to self-harm—plus a few real tactics and language to catch yourself before you call your phone a prophecy machine and mean it.
